title: The Born rule
subtitle: Probability is obtained from the squared magnitude of a quantum amplitude.
intro: A wave equation can predict how a mathematical wave changes, but it does not automatically explain what a detector records.
why: Probability is obtained from the squared magnitude of a quantum amplitude.

terms.definition: A complex coefficient of a quantum state in a chosen basis.
The predicted relative frequency of an outcome across repeated preparations.
The requirement that probabilities for all mutually exclusive outcomes sum to one.
A set of distinguishable reference states used to describe a state and its measurement.

sections.title: The missing link between waves and observations
paragraphs: A wave equation can predict how a mathematical wave changes, but it does not automatically explain what a detector records. This distinction mattered when quantum mechanics developed in the 1920s. Schrödinger provided wave mechanics, while Max Born connected wave amplitudes with probabilities of outcomes. Born’s interpretation was especially important for scattering: a calculation could describe how an incident particle interacts with a target, yet a particular detector still registered an individual event. The amplitude was not a fraction of an electron deposited in that detector. Its squared magnitude determined the probability for that event in a repeated experimental arrangement.

This is a rule connecting a state description, a measurement, and a distribution of possible results. It is not a guarantee that every finite collection reproduces that distribution exactly. If a source repeatedly prepares the same state, some outcomes may appear more often just by chance in a short run. Preparation errors and detector faults can also change results, but ordinary sampling variation does not require either explanation. The laboratory question is whether carefully collected frequencies agree with the predicted distribution within appropriate statistical uncertainty, not whether one trial reveals the entire quantum state.

sections.title: Squaring a complex number correctly
paragraphs: For an amplitude a + ib, the probability contribution is a² + b², where i² = −1. It is not the ordinary algebraic square a² + 2iab − b², which would generally be complex. The magnitude squared is the amplitude multiplied by its complex conjugate, a − ib. This produces a real, nonnegative number. Geometrically, it is the squared length of an arrow in a two-dimensional plane. Rotating that arrow without changing its length leaves its individual probability unchanged, though the rotation can matter when this amplitude is later combined with another amplitude.

Suppose a two-outcome state has coefficients 3/5 and 4i/5. Their squared magnitudes are 9/25 and 16/25. These sum to one, so the state is normalized. Measuring in that specified basis yields probabilities 0.36 and 0.64. Among 100 independent preparations, the expected counts are 36 and 64. These expectations can be non-integers for other sample sizes; they are averages over hypothetical repeated batches, not requirements imposed on each real batch. The imaginary coefficient does not mean the second outcome is imaginary or experimentally inaccessible.

sections.title: Why the measurement must be specified
paragraphs: A state does not come with one universal list of probabilities valid for every question. A measurement basis determines which amplitudes are relevant. If a qubit is in the equal superposition of zero and one, measurement in that computational basis gives equal probabilities. A measurement containing that entire superposition as one of its basis states can instead return the corresponding result with certainty. To calculate the new probabilities, first express the same state in the new basis, then apply the Born rule. Changing notation consistently does not change predictions for an unchanged physical experiment.

For continuous position, the squared magnitude of the wavefunction is a probability density, not a probability at one point. Multiplying by a small interval approximately gives its probability when the density varies slowly across that interval; integrating gives the exact result. Density therefore has units, such as inverse meters in one dimension. A density can exceed one without violating probability laws, because the integral over all positions is one. Confusing density with probability makes sharply localized wavefunctions appear paradoxical when their graphs simply use a tall, narrow area.

sections.title: What the calculator represents
paragraphs: The calculator uses two real amplitude weights and normalizes their squared values. Restricting the first weight to positive values ensures the normalization denominator never vanishes, even if the second weight is zero. The weights describe a mathematical family, not two independently calibrated detector intensities. Increasing one weight changes both normalized probabilities because the total must remain one. This is useful for checking the difference between linear weights and squared weights: weights one and two correspond to probabilities one fifth and four fifths, rather than one third and two thirds.

No plot here derives the Born rule from a deeper theory or resolves the interpretation of quantum measurement. The rule is part of the predictive framework being illustrated. More general measurements use positive operators and density matrices, but retain the same connection between the state and normalized nonnegative outcome probabilities. The central skill is to identify the appropriate amplitude, calculate its magnitude squared, and check normalization. An amplitude can cancel another amplitude before that calculation; a negative probability cannot cancel a positive one afterward. That distinction connects this lesson to interference and prevents a misleading purely classical reading of superposition.

equation.explanation: Calculate probabilities from two real unnormalized weights.

insight: Square each weight and divide by the sum: 1/(1+4)=1/5.

misconceptions.correction: Taking a squared magnitude produces a real, nonnegative probability.

misconceptions.myth: A probability density greater than one is impossible.
misconceptions.correction: A density has units; only its integral over a region is a probability bounded by one.

check.question: Weights one and two give what probability for the first outcome?
check.explanation: Square each weight and divide by the sum: 1/(1+4)=1/5.

model.title: Normalized amplitude weights
model.description: Calculate probabilities from two real unnormalized weights.
model.assumptions: A normalized pure two-state system with real weights and a computational-basis measurement. No detector noise or experimental validation is modeled.
